title: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): A Protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal
summary: Describes ICE, a protocol for NAT traversal in UDP-based communication. Endpoints gather candidate addresses, using STUN and TURN, and test which pairs actually connect. This document obsoletes RFC 5245.

plainLanguage.summary: Two kids behind locked gates want to meet. They each list every door they might use, try them all, and pick the one that works.

questions: how do webrtc peers find a connection path
how does ice nat traversal work
what is a server reflexive candidate
what is the difference between ice full and lite
subtitle: How two endpoints behind NATs try every plausible address pair until they find one that carries traffic.

tldr.problem: Peers that want to send UDP data directly to each other usually sit behind NATs, and neither knows which addresses will actually work between them.
tldr.mechanism: Each side gathers several candidate addresses (local, NAT-translated and relayed), swaps them over a signaling channel, and tests every pairing with STUN connectivity checks in priority order. The controlling side then nominates one working pair.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8445 obsoletes RFC 5245, removes aggressive nomination and is independent of any signaling protocol. It has since been updated by RFC 8863.

today: RFC 8445 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5245, and it has been updated by RFC 8863.

sections.title: The NAT Problem ICE Solves
sections.content:
Protocols that set up a communication session usually swap IP addresses and ports for the data. That is hard when a Network Address Translator (NAT) sits in the way. These protocols also want a direct flow between the peers, with no application-layer intermediary, to cut latency, reduce packet loss and lower operating costs.

Earlier fixes such as Application Layer Gateways, the Middlebox Control Protocol and Realm Specific IP each work well in some network layouts and badly in others. Admins and implementers end up assuming things about the network, which adds complexity and brittleness.

Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) takes a different route. It exchanges many addresses and ports, tests them peer to peer with STUN checks, and uses TURN as a relay of last resort. RFC 8445 describes ICE for UDP-based data streams, and notes that it has been extended to other transports such as TCP in RFC 6544. It does not provide NAT traversal for the signaling channel itself, which must come from some other mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Doors between two walled gardens are hidden, so each kid tries every door they know about until one lets them through to the other side.

sections.title: Candidates, Bases and Priorities
sections.content:
A candidate is a transport address (an IP address plus a UDP port) that an agent could use. RFC 8445 defines four types: host candidates from a local interface, server-reflexive candidates (the address a NAT shows to the outside world, learned from STUN or TURN), relayed candidates allocated on a TURN server, and peer-reflexive candidates, which are discovered later during connectivity checks. Every candidate also has a base, the address the agent actually sends from. For a host candidate the base is the candidate itself.

Each candidate gets a priority that MUST be a positive integer between 1 and (2**31 - 1). Agents SHOULD use the recommended formula priority = (2^24)*(type preference) + (2^8)*(local preference) + (2^0)*(256 - component ID). Recommended type preferences are 126 for host, 110 for peer-reflexive, 100 for server-reflexive and 0 for relayed candidates, so direct routes are tried before indirect ones.

Agents drop a candidate if its transport address and base both equal those of a higher-priority one. They also compute a foundation for each candidate, which groups candidates of the same type, base IP address, server and transport. When candidates are exchanged, the foundation is a sequence of up to 32 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kid writes a list of doors and ranks them: the front gate first, the secret tunnel last. Everyone agrees that simple, direct doors are tried first.

sections.title: Connectivity Checks and Checklists
sections.content:
Once both agents have swapped candidates, each pairs its local candidates with the remote ones. The pair priority is 2^32*MIN(G,D) + 2*MAX(G,D) + (G>D?1:0), where G is the priority of the controlling agent's candidate and D that of the controlled agent's. Pairs are sorted from high to low priority. Reflexive local candidates are replaced by their base, because an agent cannot send from them directly, and redundant pairs are pruned. The result is the checklist for that data stream.

Each check is a STUN Binding request from the local to the remote candidate. When both sides check the same pair, the result is a 4-way handshake: each side sends a request and gets a response. A successful check yields a valid pair that goes on the valid list. When an agent receives a check, it queues a triggered check on the same pair to speed things up. If a Binding response shows a mapped address the agent did not know, that address becomes a new peer-reflexive candidate.

Each pair is in one of five states: Frozen, Waiting, In-Progress, Succeeded or Failed. A checklist is Running, Completed (a nominated pair exists for every component) or Failed. To limit amplification attacks, an agent MUST cap the total number of candidate pairs; the default limit is 100 and the value MUST be configurable.
sections.plainLanguage: The kids pair up every door of theirs with every door of the other kid and test the best-looking pairs first. If a knock gets an answer, that pair is marked as working.

sections.title: Roles and Nomination
sections.content:
In each session one agent is controlling and the other controlled. If both agents are full implementations, the initiating agent is controlling. If one is a lite implementation (an agent with a public IP address that uses only host candidates and does not run checks or state machines, though it answers checks), the full agent is controlling. Roles persist for the session. If both agents claim the same role, the STUN server procedures use random tiebreaker values, and the loser is told with error 487 (Role Conflict).

The controlling agent lets checks run, then picks one valid pair and repeats its check with the USE-CANDIDATE attribute set. When that succeeds the pair is nominated, and with a nominated pair for every component the checklist is Completed and that pair becomes the selected pair. The controlling agent MUST eventually pick one and only one pair, and MUST NOT nominate another for the same component without an ICE restart.

Aggressive nomination from RFC 5245 is gone. Data may be sent on any valid pair before nomination, so there is no need to nominate continuously. Agents advertise support for this specification with the ice2 ICE option, which also stops a peer built on RFC 5245 from using aggressive nomination.
sections.plainLanguage: One kid is the captain. When enough doors work, the captain says, "We will use this one," and both kids stop testing and use only that door.

sections.title: Keepalives, Data and Restarts
sections.content:
After selection, data goes only over the selected pairs. Before that, an agent MAY send on any valid pair. If a component lacks a selected pair, the agent MUST NOT continue sending data for any component of that stream.

All endpoints MUST send keepalives to hold NAT bindings open. A keepalive goes on each pair used for data if nothing was sent for Tr seconds. Agents SHOULD use 15 seconds and MUST NOT use less. STUN keepalives use a Binding Indication with no authentication, ideally carrying only a FINGERPRINT attribute.

Either agent MAY restart ICE. A restart flushes the previous state except the roles, but data can keep flowing on existing sessions meanwhile. The agent MUST change both the username fragment and the password. Changing a stream's destination, or switching between lite and full, can only be done with a restart.
sections.plainLanguage: Every so often the kids wave through the chosen door so the guards do not lock it. If something changes, they can start the whole door-testing game again.

sections.title: Pacing and Retransmission Timers
sections.content:
STUN and TURN transactions are paced at an interval Ta, and each transaction has a retransmission timeout RTO. Agents SHOULD use a default Ta of 50 ms, but MAY pick another value based on the data. They MUST tell the peer if they want a different Ta, and both then use the higher value. All transactions from all agents combined MUST NOT go out more often than once every 5 ms.

During gathering, agents SHOULD compute RTO = MAX (500ms, Ta * (Num-Of-Cands)). For connectivity checks they SHOULD use RTO = MAX (500ms, Ta * N * (Num-Waiting + Num-In-Progress)). Agents MUST NOT use an RTO below 500 ms.

The RFC explains the effect: the first packet of every check goes out before any retransmission, which keeps a steady rate but makes ICE more sensitive to packet loss. RFC 8445 uses one set of formulas instead of the two (for real-time or not) in RFC 5245.
sections.plainLanguage: The kids do not knock on all doors at once, because that would be noisy. They knock at a steady beat and wait a fair time before knocking again.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Probing for candidates reveals the source addresses of the client and its peer to any on-network listener, and exchanging them reveals the addresses to anyone who can see the negotiation. Server-reflexive addresses gathered through a VPN user's local interface may be sensitive. Implementations where this matters are RECOMMENDED to let users control which network interfaces generate candidates.

An attacker may try to cause a false invalid result, a false valid result, a false peer-reflexive candidate, or a false valid result on a false candidate. A false peer-reflexive candidate can redirect data to a DoS target or to the attacker.

Insiders can also abuse ICE. In the STUN amplification attack, an attacker sends many candidates (say, 50) so the answering agent directs connectivity checks at a victim. In WebRTC this could be triggered in the background by malicious JavaScript. The cap on candidate pairs helps limit it.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling someone all your doors also tells them where you live, and a trickster could send you knocking on the wrong door. So ICE keeps the number of knocks limited.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 5245
sections.content:
RFC 8445 clarifies RFC 5245, fixes flaws found by implementers, and removes the SIP and SDP procedures so that ICE does not depend on any signaling protocol. Usage documents define the protocol-specific parts; the document it points to for SIP and SDP is a separate draft.

The technical changes listed in the RFC are: aggressive nomination removed, modified procedures for pair states and check scheduling, modified Ta and RTO calculation, removal of the Active and Frozen checklist definitions, the new ice2 option, modified IPv6 considerations, and removal of the no-op keepalive usage and keepalives with non-ICE peers. IANA registered four STUN attributes, one STUN error response (487) and the ice2 option.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of the rulebook. It fixes mistakes in the first one and drops a trick that turned out to be unnecessary.
